boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Groß-Glogau entry (investment and capitulation, 2 December 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the Prussian garrison of the fortress under its vice-governor, Lieutenant General Reinhart, and the Confederation of the Rhine's troops before it under Prince Jérôme, from the appearance of Lefebvre-Desnouettes' cavalry on 7 November through the investment by Deroy's Bavarian division from the 10th, the bombardments and the abandoned storm, and the blockade by the Württemberg division under Vandamme from 28 November, to the capitulation agreed on 2 December and the handover on the 3rd. The corps' formation at the start of operations, the French orders, and the suspension of arms of 16 November, which was not ratified, are context. The move of Lefebvre's and Montbrun's cavalry against Breslau from 14 November and the investment of Breslau, Bodart's separate entry, are outside this entry. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A as the Bavarians and French, 8,000 Bavarians and 1,000 French, together 9,000 men, under the Bavarian Lieutenant General v. Deroy, and side B (Prussian) as the garrison of 3,200 men with 124 guns under Lieutenant General v. Reinhart, which side A forced to surrender after a 15-day blockade; the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war, and the officers were released on their word of honour. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives the garrison's parts and total (claim side-b-strength), Davout's officer and the 32nd Bulletin other figures for it (claim side-b-strength-other), and Höpfner and the French letters and Bulletin side A's troops (claim side-a-strength). Bodart's 124 guns are Höpfner's 124; his 3,200 men are below Höpfner's 3228, so they are not Höpfner's figure rounded up as his rule states (our comparison). No passage read gives side A a total near his 9,000 or names a French troop unit before Glogau: the French named there are generals, Lefebvre-Desnouettes, Montbrun and Vandamme (our reading). His 15 days counted back from 2 December reach 17 November, while Höpfner has the place invested on 7 November and enclosed by Deroy's division on the 10th (our arithmetic and comparison). Which source Bodart used was not checked. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 2/12. investment and capitulation of Groß-Glogau'; 'the Bavarians and French (8,000 Bavarians and 1,000 French, together 9,000 men) under the Bavarian Lieutenant General v. Deroy force the Prussian garrison (3,200 men with 124 guns) under Lieutenant General v. Reinhart to surrender after a 15-day blockade'; 'the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war, the officers were released on their word of honour'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: on the day of the investment the fortress of Glogau counted in usable men the 3rd musketeer battalions of vac. Grevenitz, Tschepe and Zastrow, after the enrolment of several Ranzionirte, 2388 men; a detachment of the infantry regiment Zenge, 88; 4 invalid companies, 235; artillery, 358; Grenzjäger, 91; miners, 16; mounted cavalry from several depots, 52; together 3228 men, the greater part of them Poles who were only waiting for the first opportunity to go over to the enemy. There were 124 guns on the walls. During the investment, Höpfner adds, the unreliability of the soldiers born in South Prussia showed itself more and more, and muskets and cartridges wilfully spoiled were found with some men of Tschepe's battalion.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 18 and 25; the table's figures were checked on full-resolution crops. The garrison was in Glogau before the investment, so the claim is tagged inherited. The rows make the printed 3228 (our arithmetic); Höpfner names no source for them. 'Ranzionirte' is read as soldiers who had got away from the enemy and rejoined (our reading). The garrison's desertions and losses are in claim side-b-losses. English renderings (ours): 'on the day of the investment the fortress of Glogau counted in usable men: the 3rd musketeer battalions of vac. Grevenitz, Tschepe and Zastrow, after the enrolment of several Ranzionirte, 2388 men; a detachment of the infantry regiment Zenge 88; 4 invalid companies 235; artillery 358; Grenzjäger [frontier riflemen] 91; miners 16; mounted cavalry from several depots 52; together 3228 men, of whom the greater part were Poles, who were only waiting for the first opportunity to be able to go over to the enemy'; 'there were 124 pieces of ordnance on the walls; there was no lack either of munition or of provisions to withstand a lengthy siege; the burghers too, despite the shortness of the time, had supplied themselves with food as far as possible'; 'unfortunately the unreliability of the soldiers born in South Prussia showed itself more and more in the garrison. Muskets and cartridges wilfully spoiled were found with some men of the 3rd musketeer battalion von Tschepe'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), other figures: Marshal Davout wrote to the Emperor from Francfort on 4 November that one of his officers, sent toward Breslau with 80 horse, wrote from Beuthen on the Oder, a few leagues from Glogau, that the garrison of Glogau amounted to 3,500 men, of whom 1,000 cavalry, composed like Küstrin's of 3rd battalions, and that Major General Margitz commanded the place. The 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November: the King of Prussia had one regiment left in the place of Gross-Glogau, which was besieged.
claims.rationale: Davout's letter and the Bulletin, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. Not reconciled with Höpfner's figures or Bodart's (claims side-b-strength, bodart-strength). The garrison was in Glogau before the investment, so the claim is tagged inherited. Davout's 3,500 is above Höpfner's 3228, and his 1,000 cavalry compare with Höpfner's 52 mounted cavalry of the depots (our comparison). Davout's 'Margitz' is not a name Höpfner gives; Höpfner names Major General Marwitz as commandant of the town (claim bodart-commanders; our comparison). English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor. Francfort, 4 November 1806'; 'I received this morning a report from one of my officers whom I sent toward Breslau with 80 horse to stop the couriers and get news; he writes to me from Beuthen on the Oder, a few leagues from Glogau, that all Silesia is without Prussian' (the word continues on p. 42; the note mark refers to Foucart's footnote, not transcribed); 'troops, except the fortresses; that the garrison of Glogau amounts to 3,500 men, of whom 1,000 cavalry. It is composed, like that of Küstrin, of 3rd battalions. Major General Margitz commands the place. He is said to be very uneasy and mediocre' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 41); '32nd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'there remains today to the King of Prussia one regiment in the place of' (the sentence continues on p. 849); 'Gross-Glogau, which is besieged, one at Breslau, one at Brieg, 2 at Warsaw and some regiments at Königsberg; in all, about 15,000 men of infantry and 3 or 4,000 men of cavalry' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 848).

claims.value: Side A (the Confederation of the Rhine's troops under Prince Jérôme, with French generals). Höpfner's formation and strength at the beginning of operations: the first Bavarian division, Lieutenant General Deroy, 8185 men in the brigades of Siebein and Raglowich; the second, Lieutenant General Wrede, 5830 men in the brigades of Mezzanelli (3596) and Count Minucci; together 14,015 Bavarians; the Württemberg division, Lieutenant General Seckendorf, 8642 men; the Silesian corps 29½ battalions, 26 squadrons and 48 guns, or 17,650 men of infantry, 3241 of cavalry and 1055 of artillery, or 22,946 men; the 6th and 14th Line Infantry Regiments, the 5th light battalion La Motte and apparently several batteries arrived only later. Wrede's division reached Krossen on 4 November, Deroy's on the 7th and the Württemberg contingent on the 8th, when the corps was united. By Napoleon's order the cavalry formed 3 brigades: Mezzanelli's of the 1st Chevauxlegers and 1st Dragoons, Lefebvre-Desnouettes' of the 2nd and 3rd Chevauxlegers and 2nd Dragoons, and Montbrun's of the 3 Württemberg cavalry regiments. The first force before Glogau: Lefebvre with his brigade and a light battery on the left bank, sent on 6 November, with two squadrons of Chevauxlegers crossing to the right bank at Neusalz so that the fortress could be invested on both banks on 7 November (Höpfner); 3 cavalry regiments and 6 pieces of light artillery, with two squadrons before the bridgehead on the right bank (Foucart's narrative); 2,000 Bavarian horse (the 30th Bulletin). The major general's letter of 5 November ordered Deroy to invest Glogau with 6,000 men. Deroy's division had to advance from Krossen on 9 November so as to enclose the place on the 10th, Raglowich on the left bank and Siebein on the right (Höpfner); by the 30th Bulletin it invested Glogau on the 9th. The artillery of Wrede's division arrived on the evening of the 12th. On the 14th Lefebvre, with the 3rd Chevauxlegers and 2nd Dragoons, a Württemberg cavalry regiment and a light battery, and Montbrun with the rest of his brigade moved against Breslau, the 2nd Chevauxlegers posted halfway; Wrede's division was ordered to Polkwitz, on the road to Breslau, and the rest of the Württemberg division later to Kuttlau. The Württemberg brigade Lilienberg arrived on the right bank on 16 November and relieved Siebein on the 17th. The major general's letter of 16 November sent 2,000 Württemberg infantry, all their cavalry and 4 guns to Lissa. Deroy's division left on the 25th; the Württemberg division, about 8000 men strong, stayed, with 1 battalion on the right bank and the rest on the left from the 26th; Vandamme, entrusted with the blockade, arrived on the 28th, and Montbrun's cavalry brigade covered the blockade toward Breslau at Polkwitz. No passage read gives a return of side A at the capitulation.
claims.rationale: Höpfner and the French letters and Bulletin, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. The troops before Glogau changed with the orders of the Emperor and of Jérôme, so the phase is left unresolved. Höpfner's table does not add up in two places: the second division's rows, with the 3596 carried over, make 7018, not the printed 5830, and the Württemberg rows make 8652, not 8642; his corps figures make 21,946, not the printed 22,946, and the printed division totals, 14,015 and 8642, make 22,657; the printed 8185 and 5830 make the printed 14,015 (our arithmetic). Lefebvre's three regiments in Höpfner's table make 1097 men (our arithmetic), against the 30th Bulletin's 2,000 horse (our comparison). Höpfner's note gives a battery as 4 cannon and 2 howitzers; Foucart's narrative gives Lefebvre 6 pieces of light artillery, and the 30th Bulletin has the place bombarded on the 8th by 10 howitzers (our comparison). The 6,000 of 5 November and the 2,000 sent to Lissa are orders, not counts, and whether the Lissa detachment went is not shown. Bodart's 8,000 Bavarians and 1,000 French are in claim bodart-strength. English renderings (ours): 'the Confederation of the Rhine's troops thus coming together had the following formation and strength at the beginning of operations:'; 'First Bavarian Division. Lieutenant General Deroy. 1st Brigade, Major General Siebein: 1st Line Infantry Regiment (Leib-Regiment) 1407 men; 10th ditto (Junker) 1257; 6th light battalion Taxis 707; 2 companies of Jäger 408; 1st Chevauxlegers Regiment Kronprinz 444; 1st battery Peters 117. 2nd Brigade, Major General Raglowich: 4th Line Infantry Regiment 1576 men; 5th ditto (Preising) 1568; 1st Dragoon Regiment Minucci 435; 2nd battery Göschel 122; light battery Koppelt 144; [total] 8185 men'; 'Second Bavarian Division. Lieutenant General Wrede. 1st Brigade, Major General Mezzanelli: 2nd Line Infantry Regiment Kronprinz 1351 men; 13th ditto 1180; 3rd light battalion Preising 572; 2nd Chevauxlegers Regiment König 384; 1st battery Kaspers 109; [total] 3596 men' (the table continues on p. 16); 'carried forward 3596 men. 2nd Brigade, Major General Count Minucci: 3rd Line Infantry Regiment Herzog Karl 1269 men; 7th ditto Löwenstein 642; 4th light battalion Zoller 571; 3rd Chevauxlegers Regiment Leiningen 399; 2nd battery Vandouse 107; 2nd Dragoon Regiment Taxis 314; 12-pounder battery Tausch 120; [total] 5830 men. Together 14,015 men Bavarians'; 'Württemberg Division. Lieutenant General Seckendorf. 1st Brigade, Major General Lilienberg: Infantry Regiment Kronprinz 813 men; ditto Seckendorf 815; ditto Lilienberg 819. 2nd Brigade, Major General Schröder: Infantry Regiment Prinz Wilhelm 818 men; ditto Schröder 817. Light Brigade, Colonel Neubronn: 1st Jäger battalion Hügel 725 men; 2nd ditto Scharfenstein 744; 1st light infantry battalion Neubronn 753; 2nd ditto Brüssel 739. Lieutenant Colonel L'Estocq: 1st Chevauxlegers Regiment König 455 men; 2nd ditto 462; 1st mounted Jäger Regiment 348; horse battery Besner 130 men; foot battery Bausch 214. Together 8642 men Württembergers'; 'the Silesian corps thus consisted at the time of 29½ battalions, 26 squadrons and 48 guns, or 17,650 men' (the sentence continues on p. 17); 'infantry, 3241 men cavalry and 1055 men artillery, or 22,946 men' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 16); '1) there arrived only later the 6th and 14th Line Infantry Regiments and the 5th light battalion La Motte and, as it seems, also several batteries. The battery consisted of 4 cannon and 2 howitzers'; 'the division Wrede had arrived from Franconia by way of Schleiz and Plauen at Dresden on 25 October and had been set in march from there on the 30th by way of Hoyerswerda, Kottbus, Peiz and Guben on Krossen, which place it reached on 4 November'; 'the division Deroy, having reached Bayreuth on 21 October, reached Dresden on 2 November, after relieving the 13th Infantry Regiment before the Plassenburg by the 6th Regiment. It set out again from Dresden as early as the 3rd and reached Krossen on 7 November'; 'the Württemberg contingent reached Dresden from Ellwangen on the 3rd and Krossen on 8 November, so that on that day the corps was united'; 'by Napoleon's order the cavalry was divided into 3 brigades: under the Bavarian Major General Mezzanelli the 1st Chevauxlegers and 1st Dragoon Regiments, under Jerome's general and adjutant Lefebvre-Desnouettes the 2nd and 3rd Chevauxlegers and 2nd Dragoon Regiments, and under the French General Montbrun, whom Napoleon sent to the corps, the 3 Württemberg cavalry regiments'; 'as early as 6 November General Lefebvre had been set in march to that end with his brigade and a light battery on the left bank of the Oder against Glogau, to move the commandant to surrender by the surprising appearance of this cavalry, as had succeeded so splendidly at Erfurt and Stettin'; 'two squadrons of Chevauxlegers crossed to the right bank of the Oder at Neusalz, so as to be able to invest the fortress on both banks on 7 November'; 'on the right General Lefebvre-Desnöettes moved on the 7th before Glogau by the left bank of the Oder with 3 cavalry regiments and 6 pieces of light artillery while two squadrons appeared before the bridgehead on the right bank. The enemy's cavalry patrols were thrown back into the place' (Foucart's narrative); '30th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 10 November 1806'; 'Prince Jérôme has had the place of Glogau, capital of Upper Silesia, blockaded by Brigade General Lefebvre at the head of 2,000 Bavarian horse. The place was bombarded on the 8th by 10 howitzers served by light artillery. The Prince has praised the conduct of the Bavarian cavalry. General Deroy, with his division, invested Glogau on the 9th; talks have been opened for its surrender'; 'the Major General to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 5 November 1806'; 'the Emperor orders that Your Highness send' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'General Deroy to invest the place of Glogau with 6,000 men... Your Highness will prescribe to General Deroy to have himself scouted for and to send cavalry parties toward Breslau to intercept the couriers and learn thereby the situation of that place..... General Deroy will be before Glogau on the 7th or 8th at the latest; you on the 6th in the evening at Grüneberg; the Württembergers on the 7th at Zullichau in position' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 56; the points are the print's); 'as soon as Jerome had received General Lefebvre's report, he made all arrangements to enter Silesia now. The division Deroy had to advance from Krossen to Glogau on 9 November, so as to enclose the place on the 10th with the brigade Raglowich on the left bank and with the brigade Siebein on the right bank'; 'on 11 November the Bavarians worked on the left bank at cover for six batteries, and on the evening of the 12th the artillery of the division Wrede also arrived from Grüneberg before Glogau. At midnight the guns were brought into these earthworks, each of them, with the exception of battery No. 5, armed with 4 cannon and 2 howitzers; the said' (the sentence continues on p. 21); 'the brigade Lilienberg of the Württemberg division received the order to march on the 15th from Züllichau to Glogau' (the sentence continues on p. 23); 'to relieve the brigade Siebein, which was to unite with the brigade Raglowich on the left bank of the Oder; the division Wrede had already received the order to march on the 14th from Grüneberg to Polkwitz and to take post on the road to Breslau, and later the rest of the Württemberg division also received the order to advance on the 18th to Kuttlau. Only the corps' heavy baggage remained at Grüneberg' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 22); 'likewise on the 14th General Lefebvre advanced with the 3rd Chevauxlegers and 2nd Dragoon Regiments, a Württemberg cavalry regiment and a light battery on the left bank, and General Montbrun on the right bank of the Oder with the rest of his cavalry brigade, against Breslau, and the 2nd Chevauxlegers Regiment received the order to post itself halfway between Glogau and Breslau, to keep up the connection between this cavalry and the blockading troops'; 'on 16 November at 4½ in the morning the enemy's fire began anew on both banks of the Oder. The town burned in perhaps 30 places, but through the exemplary conduct of the burghers, supported by some men detailed for it, the fire was this time too put out everywhere'; 'on this day the Württemberg brigade Lilienberg arrived before Glogau on the right bank of the Oder'; 'on 17 November early the Bavarians set fire to the wood still standing at the Schießhaus, whereby the building itself was laid in ashes. The Württembergers relieved the brigade Siebein on this day, which moved to the left bank; a bridge at Beichau was to maintain the connection between the two banks'; 'the Major General to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'the Emperor charges me to inform Your Imperial Highness that you are to keep the Württemberg troops on the right bank of the Oder and the Bavarian troops on the left bank. Order the Württemberg troops to move before Glogau and blockade that town on the right bank; send 2,000 men of Württemberg infantry, all the cavalry of that nation and 4 pieces of artillery to Lissa, from where it will put itself in correspondence at once with the troops of Marshal Davout who are at Posen;'; 'in consequence of this the Bavarian division Deroy set out from Glogau on the 25th, crossed the Oder at Beichau and went by way of Lissa to Kalisch; the division Wrede left the hutted camp at Polkwitz, crossed the Oder at Steinau on a bridge for whose building General Montbrun, back from the expedition against Breslau, had driven the boats together, and united on the 28th with the first-named division at Kalisch, from where the two Bavarian cavalry brigades Lefebvre and Mezzanelli pushed on over the Warthe'; 'before Glogau there remained the Württemberg division, about 8000 men strong, which because of its weakness left only 1 battalion on the right bank of the Oder, but crossed with the rest to the left bank on the 26th'; 'Napoleon entrusted the continuation of the blockade to the French General Vandamme, but he arrived at Glogau only on the 28th. The cavalry brigade Montbrun secured the blockade toward Breslau by a position at Polkwitz'.

claims.value: Bodart names the Bavarian Lieutenant General v. Deroy as side A's commander and Lieutenant General v. Reinhart as side B's. Höpfner: Napoleon had given his brother Jérôme command over the Bavarian divisions of Deroy and Wrede and the Württemberg contingent; the King had named Lieutenant General Reinhart vice-governor of Glogau, where he arrived only on 30 October; Major General Marwitz was commandant of the town, Major Lichtenberg artillery officer and Captain Moritz engineer officer of the place. Deroy's division left Glogau on the 25th; Napoleon entrusted the continuation of the blockade to the French General Vandamme, who arrived on the 28th, and on 2 December, after Vandamme's general staff officer brought proposals of capitulation, agreement was soon reached. The major general's letter of 22 November ordered Deroy's division to leave on the 24th and entrusted the blockade to Vandamme and the Württemberg troops under his orders.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed commanders, read from the frame transcription, with Höpfner and the major general's letter, read from the page images. Side A's command passed during the blockade, on the Emperor's orders, from the Bavarian division before the place to Vandamme, while side B's commanders were in post before the investment; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. Bodart's Reinhart is Höpfner's vice-governor (our comparison). His Deroy commanded the Bavarian division before Glogau from 10 November, but by Höpfner and the letter of 22 November the division left before the capitulation, which Vandamme concluded (claims capitulation, side-a-command); Jérôme, to whom Napoleon gave the command of the corps, is not named by Bodart (our comparison). The credit is not assigned here to any one commander. The capitulation's text, which would show who signed it, was not seen. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'Napoleon had given his brother Jerome command over the Bavarian divisions Deroy and Wrede and over the Württemberg contingent, and had destined these troops to operate on the right wing of the Grande Armée by way of Dresden on Krossen, so as to be ready from this last point still to support the troops entering South Prussia and, as these advanced further, to be employed against the province of Silesia, which remained lying to the side'; 'the King had named Lieutenant General Reinhart vice-governor of Glogau; he had arrived there only on 30 October. Major General Marwitz was commandant of the town, Major Lichtenberg artillery officer and Captain Moritz engineer officer of the place'; 'in consequence of this the Bavarian division Deroy set out from Glogau on the 25th, crossed the Oder at Beichau and went by way of Lissa to Kalisch; the division Wrede left the hutted camp at Polkwitz, crossed the Oder at Steinau on a bridge for whose building General Montbrun, back from the expedition against Breslau, had driven the boats together, and united on the 28th with the first-named division at Kalisch, from where the two Bavarian cavalry brigades Lefebvre and Mezzanelli pushed on over the Warthe'; 'Napoleon entrusted the continuation of the blockade to the French General Vandamme, but he arrived at Glogau only on the 28th. The cavalry brigade Montbrun secured the blockade toward Breslau by a position at Polkwitz'; 'on 2 December the government now had new points of capitulation drafted, without calling the prescribed formal council of war, and when at noon the copies were not yet ready, an officer was sent to General Vandamme to apologise for this delay. The officer sent returned with General Vandamme's general staff officer and proposals of capitulation that agreed in essentials with those of the government. Agreement was therefore now reached very soon, and that same evening the Breslau and Oder gates were occupied by the Württembergers'; 'the Major General to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 22 November 1806, one o'clock in the afternoon'; 'the Emperor orders you to have General Deroy's Bavarian division leave, on the 24th, the position it occupies before Glogau to go to Kalisch, where His Majesty's intention is that it arrive on the 27th or 28th'; 'His Majesty orders that the blockade of Glogau be entrusted to General Vandamme and to the Württemberg troops under his orders'.

claims.value: Höpfner: Lefebvre advanced with the cavalry in regimental echelons against the glacis while the light battery fired from the Protestant churchyard and threw some shells into the town; driven back by canister toward Prostau, the cavalry enclosed the fortress on both banks and summoned it by two parlementaires, and Lefebvre, seeing that he could achieve nothing with cavalry alone, reported to headquarters and had two earthworks raised in the night by country people. On 8 November the cannonade went on; the engineer officer with the detachment found the place in a state that permitted a forcible attack but, the corps' troops being too little known, asked only for 5-6 batteries of 8-10 guns, above all high-angle pieces; at 11 o'clock there was a new parley with the news that Stettin and Küstrin had fallen. On Lefebvre's report Jérôme had the place enclosed on the 10th. Immediately after side A's fire of the 13th its artillery was withdrawn from the cover, which only infantry pickets held, with posts pushed forward and stronger infantry detachments with light artillery placed out of cannon range; after these arrangements Lefebvre, with a Bavarian officer, summoned the fortress for the third and last time in Jérôme's name, Jérôme having moved his headquarters to Ziebern; on its refusal Jérôme had siege guns brought up and the munition replenished, and a further summons threatened to lay waste the town and announced the surrender of Küstrin and Magdeburg. Deserters' news led Jérôme to plan a coup de main for the night to the 17th; with fascines and ladders ready, Deroy declared that he could not count on his troops for it, and the storm was given up to await the siege guns; Berthier answered Jérôme's report that Deroy's observations were very just. The infantry's approach in small pits from the 19th was made on Napoleon's order, to unsettle the garrison; pressed by Napoleon, Jérôme was about to attempt the bridgehead on the right bank when he received the order to leave only one division before Glogau. Vandamme, arriving on the 28th, summoned the fortress and was refused; after the bombardment of 1 December he summoned it again with the assurance that no relief could be hoped for and gave his word of honour in writing; he rejected a capitulation with free withdrawal, and his general staff officer brought proposals that agreed in essentials with the government's.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images. These were the steps of side A's commanders before Glogau, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner cites no document for Lefebvre's report, the engineer officer's judgement or the summonses, and prints Berthier's answer on the storm only in a footnote. The French orders that set these steps are in claim side-a-objectives. English renderings (ours): 'General Lefebvre advanced with the cavalry in regimental echelons against the glacis, while the light battery opened its fire at the Protestant churchyard and threw some shells into the town'; 'the canister fire from the works drove the Bavarian cavalry back toward Prostau, and they contented themselves with enclosing the fortress on both banks and summoning it by two parlementaires. The governor rejected the proposals'; 'General Lefebvre soon recognised that he would achieve nothing with the cavalry alone, and reported at once to headquarters on the result of his mission, but used the night to have two earthworks raised by country people brought together, to cover the guns he had brought with him'; 'on the morning of 8 November at 6 o'clock the cannonade against the fortress was continued, during which the' (the sentence continues on p. 20); 'engineer officer attached to the detachment reconnoitred the place and found it in a state that well permitted a forcible attack. Since, however, the troops of the corps were too little known as to their competence to entrust them with an undertaking still so hazardous, he asked only for the building of 5-6 batteries of 8-10 guns, above all high-angle pieces, to bombard works and town' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 19); 'at 11 o'clock, after the cannonade, there was a parley anew, with the communication that Stettin and Küstrin had fallen and the Prussian army was shattered'; 'as soon as Jerome had received General Lefebvre's report, he made all arrangements to enter Silesia now. The division Deroy had to advance from Krossen to Glogau on 9 November, so as to enclose the place on the 10th with the brigade Raglowich on the left bank and with the brigade Siebein on the right bank'; 'on the 13th at 4 in the morning the enemy opened his fire on both banks, although the darkness allowed aiming only at the fire of the fortress batteries, which answered with liveliness. The town burned in thirteen different places, but everywhere the fires were soon put out'; 'immediately after the end of the fire the enemy withdrew his artillery from the cover and occupied it only with infantry pickets; posts were pushed forward, and stronger infantry detachments with light artillery were placed out of cannon range'; 'after these arrangements General Lefebvre, accompanied by a Bavarian officer, was sent as parlementaire to the fortress, to summon it for the third and last time in the name of Jerome, who had moved his headquarters to Ziebern near Glogau'; 'when Jerome became aware from the Prussian government's answer that the fortress would let it come to more serious measures for its capture, he at once had every effort made to bring up siege guns and above all to replenish the munition, so that the fire could be reopened in the night to the 15th'; 'a further summons, in which Jerome declared that he would lay waste the town in the most terrible manner if the capitulation were not accepted, and at the same time communicated army orders announcing the surrender of Küstrin and Magdeburg, was again rejected'; 'it was deserters, too, who brought the enemy the most exact news of the state of the works, so that Jerome formed the plan of taking the fortress by a coup de main in the night to the 17th'; 'fascines, ladders etc., everything lay ready, when at the moment of execution General Deroy declared that he did not believe he could count on his troops for so doubtful an undertaking, since they, not used to such hazardous attacks, might easily lack the boldness and energy that alone make success certain. The storm had to be given up and the siege guns awaited'; '1) on Jerome's report of the abandonment of the storm Napoleon had Marshal Berthier answer: "I have put your letter before the Emperor, Monseigneur; His Majesty finds that the observations General Deroy made to you are very just; one cannot take a town by assault when one has not made the breach and when there is an escarp and a good counterscarp; His Majesty thinks that those who could be of the opinion of such an attack were very greatly wrong; for one would lose many men uselessly there."'; 'the enemy gradually approached the works with his infantry in small pits and opened his musket fire on the 19th, so that the bullets flew into the town'; 'these arrangements on the enemy's side had been made on Napoleon's order, to unsettle the garrison day and night thereby and make it worn down and inclined to surrender'; 'continually pressed by Napoleon to hasten the capture of Glogau, Jerome was about to attempt an attack on the bridgehead on the right bank of the Oder; but circumstances arose that prevented the execution. Jerome received, that is, the order to leave only one division before Glogau and to set out with the rest of the corps with all speed against Kalisch'; 'as soon as General Vandamme had arrived on the afternoon of the 28th, he had the fortress summoned, but was rejected'; 'on 1 December at 6¼ in the morning the bombardment began and lasted until after 9 o'clock. The garrison's artillery had indeed answered with vigour, but the enemy had achieved his purpose. The certainty that siege guns had arrived, that the enemy had it in his power to burn the town to ashes, had completely changed the government's mind'; 'immediately after the end of the fire General Vandamme sent a parlementaire anew and summoned the fortress with the assurance that no relief was to be hoped for, since neither a Prussian nor a Russian army stood on this side of the Vistula and the King of Prussia was already in Russia. Since the governor would not believe these statements, the French general gave his word of honour in writing for further confirmation'; 'although the governor had shortly before fallen out with Major Puttlitz over entering into a capitulation and on that occasion had declared that he would let himself be buried under the ruins of the town, he now nevertheless proposed to the enemy a capitulation with free withdrawal. General Vandamme rejected this proposal, and the governor promised to make other proposals the next day'; 'on 2 December the government now had new points of capitulation drafted, without calling the prescribed formal council of war, and when at noon the copies were not yet ready, an officer was sent to General Vandamme to apologise for this delay. The officer sent returned with General Vandamme's general staff officer and proposals of capitulation that agreed in essentials with those of the government. Agreement was therefore now reached very soon, and that same evening the Breslau and Oder gates were occupied by the Württembergers'.

claims.value: Höpfner: the garrison put its most reliable battalion, Grevenitz's, on the weakest places of the main wall on the left bank, Tschepe's on the rest and the worst, Zastrow's, in the Dom-Retranchement on the right bank, a detachment of the best invalids in the Sternschanze and the rest of the invalids in its gorge; the cavalry and Jäger patrolled the abandoned outworks, and the burghers did duty in the town. On 7 November the foot and mounted Jäger and the cavalry reconnoitred toward Herrendorf and fell back after losing 4 prisoners, and the governor rejected the first summonses. All works, sorties and the like that could give occasion for desertion were stopped. To the summons after the fire of 13 November the governor answered, by French statements, that he recognised the impossibility of defending himself and would lay the points of capitulation before a council of war, and asked for a written summons; the council of war, despite the artillery officer's statements on the bad carriages and deficient serving of the guns, rejected surrender, and Major Puttlitz, commander of the 3rd musketeer battalion of vac. Grevenitz, who had spoken most decidedly against capitulating, carried the refusal at 2 in the afternoon of the 14th; burghers who asked the government to surrender the town got no answer. A further summons was refused. On 18 November a detachment under the engineer officer raided the Grundmühle. From the 19th the engineer urged the artillery officer in vain to fire canister at the enemy's pits, which the artillery officer called a useless waste of munition. On 22 November Lieutenant Sommerfeld took the Zenge detachment into the nearest outworks and, on the engineer's proposal, a 12-pounder was put into the counterguard of the Prussian ravelin, while the Jäger went into the outworks to the right of the ravelin. On the 28th a plot in Tschepe's battalion was discovered, its ringleaders shot and the rest made to run the gauntlet; Vandamme's summons of that day was refused. The bombardment of 1 December completely changed the government's mind; the governor, who had shortly before quarrelled with Puttlitz over capitulating and declared that he would be buried under the ruins of the town, proposed a capitulation with free withdrawal, and on 2 December the government had new points drafted without calling the prescribed formal council of war. Höpfner gives the government's reasons as the insufficiency of the garrison for the works that had to be held, the unreliability of the 3rd battalions of Tschepe and Zastrow, made up of Poles, whose commanders said they could no longer rely on their men, the arrival of the siege guns, which made the complete ruin of the town unavoidable, and the impossibility of relief. He judges that these reasons could not justify a capitulation, since the government knew the investing troops were comparatively very weak and the royal order of 2 November communicated to it demanded a defence to the last man, and that the governor rejected every proposal while only the soldier's losses were at stake but resolved on surrender as soon as the first bombs threatened the town and the welfare of 10,000 inhabitants.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 18-31. These were the decisions of the governor, the government and the garrison's officers, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner cites no document for the councils, marks the governor's answer of the 13th as given by French statements, and prints in a footnote a letter of refusal (claim side-b-objectives); the judgement is his own. English renderings (ours): 'the most reliable battalion of the garrison, the battalion von Grevenitz, occupied the weakest places of the main wall on the left bank of the Oder, the less reliable battalion von Tschepe the rest of it, and the worst battalion, von Zastrow, the Dom-Retranchement [the cathedral entrenchment] on the right bank of the Oder; a detachment of the best invalids held the Sternschanze [star fort] at the fortress's upper junction with the Oder, the rest of the invalids occupied the gorge' (the sentence continues on p. 19); 'of this work; the cavalry and the Jäger were used to patrol the abandoned outworks. The burghers did duty in the town' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 18); 'on 7 November at 2 in the afternoon mounted messengers from the neighbouring villages brought the report that the enemy was approaching, and at 3½ the foot and mounted Jäger and the cavalry moved out in the direction of Herrendorf to reconnoitre'; 'this detachment was a few thousand paces from the works when it already came upon numerous troops of enemy cavalry, and had to fall back on the fortress after the loss of 4 prisoners'; 'the canister fire from the works drove the Bavarian cavalry back toward Prostau, and they contented themselves with enclosing the fortress on both banks and summoning it by two parlementaires. The governor rejected the proposals'; 'on the garrison's side all works, sorties etc. that could give occasion for desertion were stopped, since the losses by desertion would very soon have weakened the garrison to the utmost'; 'on the 13th at 4 in the morning the enemy opened his fire on both banks, although the darkness allowed aiming only at the fire of the fortress batteries, which answered with liveliness. The town burned in thirteen different places, but everywhere the fires were soon put out'; 'the governor answered, according to French statements, that he recognised the impossibility of defending himself, and that he would at once call a council of war and lay the points of capitulation before it; at the same time he asked for a written summons, which was given him forthwith'; 'the council of war met, but despite the statements of the place's artillery officer on the bad state of the gun carriages and the deficient serving of the guns, the' (the sentence continues on p. 22); 'surrender was rejected' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 21); 'the brave Major Puttlitz, commander of the 3rd musketeer battalion of vac. Grevenitz, who had spoken out most decidedly against the capitulation, was charged at 2 in the afternoon of the 14th with carrying the refusal to the enemy'; 'on the same day some burghers asked the government to surrender the town, but received no answer'; 'a further summons, in which Jerome declared that he would lay waste the town in the most terrible manner if the capitulation were not accepted, and at the same time communicated army orders announcing the surrender of Küstrin and Magdeburg, was again rejected'; 'on 18 November the fortress artillery tried to set on fire the water mill lying nearest the Sternschanze, the so-called Grundmühle, which gave shelter to a Bavarian post, but did not achieve its aim'; 'under the lead of the place's engineer officer a detachment of 1 officer, 40 men of the 3rd battalion von Grevenitz and some artillerymen with pitch wreaths went forward to the mill, quickly occupied the exit of the buildings, took prisoner after slight resistance the enemy post, surprised, of 1 officer and 23 men of the 4th Line Regiment, set the buildings on fire and returned to the fortress. The miller, however, managed to save the mill'; 'the enemy gradually approached the works with his infantry in small pits and opened his musket fire on the 19th, so that the bullets flew into the town'; 'in the following days this fire was continued, and in vain the place's engineer tried to move the artillery officer to hinder the enemy from continuing his digging in, and to damp his fire, by lively canister fire. The artillery officer declared this a useless waste of munition, so that the enemy fire came ever nearer and became ever more regular, at times also supported by shell fire'; 'at last on 22 November, when the enemy had approached with his pits especially along the avenue of Rauschwitz, Lieutenant Sommerfeld was sent forward with the detachment of the regiment Zenge into the nearest outworks, and on the proposal of the place's engineer a 12-pounder was brought into the counterguard of the Prussian ravelin, so as to take the' (the sentence continues on p. 27); 'advanced enemy in flank and rear. To the same end the garrison's Jäger went into the outworks to the right of the ravelin toward the Oder. The enemy infantry fire was markedly quenched by this and in the following days kept up only moderately' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 26); 'on the 28th another plot was discovered in the 3rd musketeer' (the word continues on p. 28); 'battalion von Tschepe; the ringleaders were shot, the other men punished by running the gauntlet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 27); 'as soon as General Vandamme had arrived on the afternoon of the 28th, he had the fortress summoned, but was rejected'; 'on 1 December at 6¼ in the morning the bombardment began and lasted until after 9 o'clock. The garrison's artillery had indeed answered with vigour, but the enemy had achieved his purpose. The certainty that siege guns had arrived, that the enemy had it in his power to burn the town to ashes, had completely changed the government's mind'; 'although the governor had shortly before fallen out with Major Puttlitz over entering into a capitulation and on that occasion had declared that he would let himself be buried under the ruins of the town, he now nevertheless proposed to the enemy a capitulation with free withdrawal. General Vandamme rejected this proposal, and the governor promised to make other proposals the next day'; 'on 2 December the government now had new points of capitulation drafted, without calling the prescribed formal council of war, and when at noon the copies were not yet ready, an officer was sent to General Vandamme to apologise for this delay. The officer sent returned with General Vandamme's general staff officer and proposals of capitulation that agreed in essentials with those of the government. Agreement was therefore now reached very soon, and that same evening the Breslau and Oder gates were occupied by the Württembergers'; 'the reasons that moved the government to surrender were the following: 1) the insufficiency of the garrison for the defence of the works that necessarily had to be held; 2) the unreliability of the 3rd battalions of Tschepe and Zastrow, made up of Poles, whose commanders had themselves declared that they could no longer rely on their men; 3) the arrival of the enemy's siege guns, by which the complete ruin of the town would have been unavoidable, and 4) the impossibility of a relief'; 'even if these reasons must in themselves be recognised as correct, they have not the slightest force to justify a capitulation, since the government knew that the investing troops were comparatively very weak, and the royal order of 2 November communicated to it expressly demanded a defence to the last man'; 'so long as it was only a question in Glogau of losses that fell on the soldier, the governor rejected every proposal to surrender; but as soon as the first bombs fell in the town, threatened it with devastation, and the welfare of 10,000 inhabitants was in danger, misgivings set in, and the surrender was resolved'.

claims.value: Bodart records the investment and capitulation of Groß-Glogau on 2 December: the Bavarians and French under Deroy forced the Prussian garrison under Reinhart to surrender after a 15-day blockade; the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war, the officers released on their word of honour. Höpfner: on 2 December the government had new points of capitulation drafted, Vandamme's general staff officer brought proposals that agreed with them in essentials, agreement was soon reached, and that evening the Württembergers occupied the Breslau and Oder gates; a mutiny then broke out in part of the garrison, which broke open the Jesuit church, where the stores of several cavalry depots and the effects of many private persons were kept, until the quiet part of the garrison put it down by force of arms. On 3 December the fortress was formally handed over: the troops marched out and laid down on the glacis their muskets, mostly broken beforehand; the invalids were released and the remaining men transported as prisoners of war. So fell Glogau, without the enemy having opened any siege works or dared a storm; the walls had suffered nothing, the damage to the burghers' houses was comparatively slight, and the fortress artillery was in completely good condition. The Emperor wrote to the Grand Duke of Berg from Posen on 3 December that Glogau had surrendered.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's and the Emperor's accounts, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription); no source read gives a different result. The capitulation's text was not seen; its terms are Höpfner's summary and Bodart's. Bodart's date, 2 December, is the day Höpfner has the capitulation agreed and the gates occupied; the formal handover is 3 December in Höpfner (our comparison). Bodart's release of the officers on parole is not in Höpfner, who has the invalids released and the rest taken as prisoners of war (claim side-b-losses). Höpfner's statement that side A opened no siege works stands beside his own account of its trenches and pits (claim fortification). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'on 2 December the government now had new points of capitulation drafted, without calling the prescribed formal council of war, and when at noon the copies were not yet ready, an officer was sent to General Vandamme to apologise for this delay. The officer sent returned with General Vandamme's general staff officer and proposals of capitulation that agreed in essentials with those of the government. Agreement was therefore now reached very soon, and that same evening the Breslau and Oder gates were occupied by the Württembergers'; 'until this moment the garrison had kept quiet, but now a mutiny broke out among part of it, in which the Jesuit church, where the stores of several cavalry depots and the effects of many private persons brought there for safety were kept, was broken open and many excesses committed, until it was put down by force of arms by the quiet part of the garrison'; 'on 3 December the fortress was formally handed over. The troops marched out and laid down on the glacis their muskets, which had mostly been broken beforehand. The invalids were released, the remaining men transported as prisoners of war'; 'so fell Glogau, without the enemy having opened any siege works or dared a storm. The walls had suffered nothing at all; the damage to the burghers' houses was comparatively slight; the fortress artillery was in completely good condition, despite the place's artillery officer having stated the contrary;' (the sentence continues on p. 30); 'the Emperor to the Grand Duke of Berg. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'Glogau has surrendered'.

claims.value: Side A's losses in the passages read are partial. Höpfner: on 18 November a sortie took prisoner the Bavarian post at the Grundmühle, 1 officer and 23 men of the 4th Line Regiment; on 16 November battery No. 4 and the batteries on the right bank kept up their fire until 10 o'clock without suffering any loss. claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. They cover only parts of the investment and are not a total; Bodart's entry gives no loss for side A (claim bodart-strength). No passage read gives side A's loss in the bombardments of 13, 15 and 16 November and 1 December, or from the garrison's fire on the pits from the 19th and on 22 November. English renderings (ours): 'on 18 November the fortress artillery tried to set on fire the water mill lying nearest the Sternschanze, the so-called Grundmühle, which gave shelter to a Bavarian post, but did not achieve its aim'; 'under the lead of the place's engineer officer a detachment of 1 officer, 40 men of the 3rd battalion von Grevenitz and some artillerymen with pitch wreaths went forward to the mill, quickly occupied the exit of the buildings, took prisoner after slight resistance the enemy post, surprised, of 1 officer and 23 men of the 4th Line Regiment, set the buildings on fire and returned to the fortress. The miller, however, managed to save the mill'; 'on 16 November at 4½ in the morning the enemy's fire began anew on both banks of the Oder. The town burned in perhaps 30 places, but through the exemplary conduct of the burghers, supported by some men detailed for it, the fire was this time too put out everywhere'; 'the fortress artillery answered still more decidedly than on the previous day, especially with canister and high-angle fire, so that the enemy gave the order to withdraw the guns from the cover before daybreak. A countermand of this order, to keep up by continued fire the blaze that had broken out in the town, found the batteries, except No. 4, already evacuated, so that only the latter and those on the right bank continued the fire until 10 o'clock, without suffering any loss, although the fortress artillery concentrated its fire against battery No. 4'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) lost the fortress and its garrison. Höpfner: the garrison's loss came to 30-40 dead, as many wounded, and about 200 deserters; in the night to the 28th a plot of 96 men of the 3rd musketeer battalion von Zastrow went over to the enemy, having blown up the Dom gate, barriers and drawbridges, the Zerbau redoubt and the bridge over the old Oder, wounded the artillerymen in the redoubt or forced them to desert, and spiked its cannon; on 7 November the reconnaissance lost 4 prisoners. At the handover on 3 December the troops laid down their muskets, mostly broken beforehand, the invalids were released and the remaining men transported as prisoners of war; the walls had suffered nothing, the fortress artillery was in completely good condition, and munition and provisions were present in abundance. Bodart: the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war, the officers released on their word of honour. The Emperor wrote on 3 December that Glogau had surrendered and that he had ordered 4,000 muskets to be sent from it to Warsaw to arm the Poles.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription), not combined. Höpfner does not say whether his 200 deserters include the 96 of the night to the 28th, or how many men were taken prisoner or released; no passage read counts the guns, muskets or stores taken, apart from the Emperor's 4,000 muskets. Höpfner's 3228 men and 124 guns before the investment are in claim side-b-strength. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'on 7 November at 2 in the afternoon mounted messengers from the neighbouring villages brought the report that the enemy was approaching, and at 3½ the foot and mounted Jäger and the cavalry moved out in the direction of Herrendorf to reconnoitre'; 'this detachment was a few thousand paces from the works when it already came upon numerous troops of enemy cavalry, and had to fall back on the fortress after the loss of 4 prisoners'; 'so fell Glogau, without the enemy having opened any siege works or dared a storm. The walls had suffered nothing at all; the damage to the burghers' houses was comparatively slight; the fortress artillery was in completely good condition, despite the place's artillery officer having stated the contrary;' (the sentence continues on p. 30); 'munition and provisions were present in abundance; the loss of the garrison came to 30-40 dead, as many wounded, and about 200 deserters' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 29); 'in the night to the 28th a plot of 96 men of the 3rd musketeer battalion von Zastrow went over to the enemy. The deserters had blown up the Dom gate, the barriers and drawbridges, the Zerbau redoubt and the bridge over the old Oder, partly wounded the artillerymen in the redoubt, partly forced them to desert, and spiked the cannon there'; 'on 3 December the fortress was formally handed over. The troops marched out and laid down on the glacis their muskets, which had mostly been broken beforehand. The invalids were released, the remaining men transported as prisoners of war'; 'the Emperor to the Grand Duke of Berg. Posen, 3 December 1806'; 'Glogau has surrendered'; 'I have ordered that 4,000 muskets be sent from that place to Warsaw to arm the Poles'.

claims.value: Bodart places Groß-Glogau, a town in Prussia, province of Silesia, on the Oder, 50 km north of Liegnitz; the 30th Bulletin calls Glogau the capital of Upper Silesia. Höpfner: the fortress lay on both banks of the Oder, with its main wall on the left bank, the Dom-Retranchement on the right bank and the Sternschanze at its upper junction with the Oder; the Schießhaus, a farmstead, stood close below the town on the Oder; side A approached especially along the avenue of Rauschwitz; the batteries on the right bank stood behind the dam before Zerbau; a bridge at Beichau was to keep the connection between the banks; and on 30 November the roads were so bad from the wet weather that the small mortars and the howitzers, brought up on sledges, could be put into the batteries only at 8 in the evening.
claims.rationale: Location and works as described, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription). Höpfner's Plan Nr. XVII of Glogau was not inspected, and where each work stood is taken only from the descriptions; the works themselves are in claim fortification. The 30th Bulletin's 'capital of Upper Silesia' is kept as printed. The ground is tagged inherited; the weather and the roads are kept with it. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, province of Silesia, on the Oder, 50 km north of Liegnitz)'; '30th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 10 November 1806'; 'Prince Jérôme has had the place of Glogau, capital of Upper Silesia, blockaded by Brigade General Lefebvre at the head of 2,000 Bavarian horse. The place was bombarded on the 8th by 10 howitzers served by light artillery. The Prince has praised the conduct of the Bavarian cavalry. General Deroy, with his division, invested Glogau on the 9th; talks have been opened for its surrender'; 'the most reliable battalion of the garrison, the battalion von Grevenitz, occupied the weakest places of the main wall on the left bank of the Oder, the less reliable battalion von Tschepe the rest of it, and the worst battalion, von Zastrow, the Dom-Retranchement [the cathedral entrenchment] on the right bank of the Oder; a detachment of the best invalids held the Sternschanze [star fort] at the fortress's upper junction with the Oder, the rest of the invalids occupied the gorge' (the sentence continues on p. 19); 'of this work; the cavalry and the Jäger were used to patrol the abandoned outworks. The burghers did duty in the town' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 18); 'during this cannonade the enemy set fire in several places to the stock of wood of 10-15,000 Klafter [cords] standing by the Schießhaus [shooting house], a farmstead close below the town on the Oder'; 'at last on 22 November, when the enemy had approached with his pits especially along the avenue of Rauschwitz, Lieutenant Sommerfeld was sent forward with the detachment of the regiment Zenge into the nearest outworks, and on the proposal of the place's engineer a 12-pounder was brought into the counterguard of the Prussian ravelin, so as to take the' (the sentence continues on p. 27); 'battery received only 2 cannon and 1 howitzer. On the right bank only ½ a Bavarian battery and a Württemberg battery brought up, or 9 guns, had been placed behind the dam to the left before Zerbau' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 20); 'on 17 November early the Bavarians set fire to the wood still standing at the Schießhaus, whereby the building itself was laid in ashes. The Württembergers relieved the brigade Siebein on this day, which moved to the left bank; a bridge at Beichau was to maintain the connection between the two banks'; 'on the evening of the same day six vessels with siege guns and munition arrived at Beichau. On 29 November the unloading of the projectiles began, which were housed in the church of Prostau; on the 30th the guns, 6 small and 4 heavy mortars and 4 howitzers of heavy calibre, were disembarked, but the roads had become so bad from the wet weather that had set in that only in the evening at 8 o'clock could the small mortars and the howitzers, brought up on sledges, be put into the batteries, and, together with the field howitzers already standing there, the following distribution took place: in battery No. 1, 2 mortars and 2 howitzers; in No. 2, 3 and 5, 2 howitzers each; in No. 4 and 6, 2 mortars and 2 howitzers each'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: 124 guns stood on the walls, and there was no lack of munition or provisions for a lengthy siege; the burghers too had laid in food. During the investment the garrison was very well fed: burghers sent warm meals to the walls, a collection was made for the artillerymen, few in number and heavily worked, and the Jewish community gave 100 coats, so that with the clothing stores of the cavalry depots most of the men on duty had coats. Side A dug off the pipes that brought the town's drinking water, so that pumps were set in the Oder. At the council of war the artillery officer spoke of the bad carriages and deficient serving of the guns; at the fall the fortress artillery was in good condition and munition and provisions were present in abundance. Side A: the Emperor wrote on 10 November that he had ordered the general commanding at Küstrin to embark 6 mortars and 4 siege howitzers for Glogau, and that all the boats on the Oder should be collected for a bridge. Höpfner: the batteries were armed with 4 cannon and 2 howitzers each, battery No. 5 with 2 cannon and 1 howitzer, with 9 guns on the right bank; after the refusal Jérôme had siege guns brought up and the munition replenished, and the batteries were rearmed with 12-pounders and howitzers, battery No. 6 being given up; the mortars and heavy howitzers expected from Küstrin, embarked on the 14th, were held up by the water level of the Oder; six vessels with siege guns and munition reached Beichau on the evening of the 28th, and on the 30th 6 small and 4 heavy mortars and 4 heavy howitzers were disembarked, with 30 rounds ready for the siege guns and 40 for the field howitzers, while the 4 heavy mortars could not yet be brought up. The major general's letter of 16 November ordered a bridge over the Oder near Glogau and, since Lissa and the other towns in that part must have much grain, a requisition of 100,000 rations of oats and 20,000 quintals of wheat or flour, to be sent to Posen. Höpfner has the corps' heavy baggage remain at Grüneberg.
claims.rationale: Höpfner and the French letters, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. Side B's guns and stores were set before the investment, side A's guns and supplies came from the commanders' dispositions; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. The Emperor's 6 mortars and 4 howitzers ordered and Höpfner's 6 small and 4 heavy mortars and 4 heavy howitzers disembarked are kept as given (our comparison). Whether the requisition of 16 November was made is not shown. No passage read counts side A's daily needs or the stores found at the capitulation. English renderings (ours): 'there were 124 pieces of ordnance on the walls; there was no lack either of munition or of provisions to withstand a lengthy siege; the burghers too, despite the shortness of the time, had supplied themselves with food as far as possible'; 'the garrison meanwhile was very well fed'; 'a great part of the burghers sent the troops on the walls warm breakfast, even dinner, and a collection was made throughout the town for the artillerymen, who because of their small number had an especially heavy service'; 'to protect the soldiers better against the raw weather, the burghers set up fair booths behind the walls; indeed even the numerous Jewish community collected and gave the garrison 100 coats, so that, with the help of the clothing stores of the cavalry depots, the men on duty could for the most part be provided with coats'; 'it was felt very keenly that the enemy dug off the pipes by which the town was supplied with drinking water, so that pumps had to be set in the Oder to make do with river water'; 'the council of war met, but despite the statements of the place's artillery officer on the bad state of the gun carriages and the deficient serving of the guns, the' (the sentence continues on p. 22); 'surrender was rejected' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 21); 'so fell Glogau, without the enemy having opened any siege works or dared a storm. The walls had suffered nothing at all; the damage to the burghers' houses was comparatively slight; the fortress artillery was in completely good condition, despite the place's artillery officer having stated the contrary;' (the sentence continues on p. 30); 'munition and provisions were present in abundance; the loss of the garrison came to 30-40 dead, as many wounded, and about 200 deserters' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 29); 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 10 November 1806'; 'I greatly wish to be master of Glogau. I have given orders to the general commanding at Küstrin to embark 6 mortars and 4 siege howitzers and to send them to you to bombard the town. If Glogau surrenders, send an officer to inform Küstrin of it, so that this movement is not made'; 'have all the boats you come upon on the Oder collected, so as to make a bridge in one night and wherever you wish'; 'on 11 November the Bavarians worked on the left bank at cover for six batteries, and on the evening of the 12th the artillery of the division Wrede also arrived from Grüneberg before Glogau. At midnight the guns were brought into these earthworks, each of them, with the exception of battery No. 5, armed with 4 cannon and 2 howitzers; the said' (the sentence continues on p. 21); 'battery received only 2 cannon and 1 howitzer. On the right bank only ½ a Bavarian battery and a Württemberg battery brought up, or 9 guns, had been placed behind the dam to the left before Zerbau' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 20); 'when Jerome became aware from the Prussian government's answer that the fortress would let it come to more serious measures for its capture, he at once had every effort made to bring up siege guns and above all to replenish the munition, so that the fire could be reopened in the night to the 15th'; 'the gun cover was built more solidly, and since the fortress's 6-pounders did no damage but did betray the weakness of the blockading troops' artillery, it was decided to restrict themselves more to the use of the howitzers and 12-pounders and to arm the batteries accordingly, so that batteries No. 2, 3 and 4 were each equipped with two 12-pounders and 2 howitzers, battery No. 1 with two 12-pounders, and only battery No. 5 with two 6-pounders and 1 howitzer, while battery No. 6 was given up entirely'; 'in the night to the 18th the blockading troops worked on the left bank of the Oder at trenches about 100 paces long, to the right and left of the several batteries, so as to place in them 200 men of infantry each to cover the artillery,' (the sentence continues on p. 26); 'and everything was prepared for setting up the mortars and heavy howitzers expected from Küstrin, which had been embarked on the 14th but were held up by the water level of the Oder' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 25); 'as soon as General Vandamme had arrived on the afternoon of the 28th, he had the fortress summoned, but was rejected'; 'on the evening of the same day six vessels with siege guns and munition arrived at Beichau. On 29 November the unloading of the projectiles began, which were housed in the church of Prostau; on the 30th the guns, 6 small and 4 heavy mortars and 4 howitzers of heavy calibre, were disembarked, but the roads had become so bad from the wet weather that had set in that only in the evening at 8 o'clock could the small mortars and the howitzers, brought up on sledges, be put into the batteries, and, together with the field howitzers already standing there, the following distribution took place: in battery No. 1, 2 mortars and 2 howitzers; in No. 2, 3 and 5, 2 howitzers each; in No. 4 and 6, 2 mortars and 2 howitzers each'; 'for the siege guns 30, for the field howitzers 40 rounds lay ready in the batteries. By night the town was to be shelled, by day partly the town, partly the cavaliers of the fortress and the embrasures of the works. The 4 heavy mortars had not yet been brought up'; 'the Major General to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'the Emperor wishes you to have a bridge thrown over the Oder near Glogau; this bridge will have the double advantage of favouring your blockade and giving you the means of moving rapidly from one bank to the other'; 'the town of Lissa and the other towns in that part must have much grain; the Emperor therefore wishes you to make a requisition of 100,000 rations of oats, 20,000 quintals of wheat or flour and to have them sent as soon as possible to Posen'; 'the brigade Lilienberg of the Württemberg division received the order to march on the 15th from Züllichau to Glogau' (the sentence continues on p. 23); 'to relieve the brigade Siebein, which was to unite with the brigade Raglowich on the left bank of the Oder; the division Wrede had already received the order to march on the 14th from Grüneberg to Polkwitz and to take post on the road to Breslau, and later the rest of the Württemberg division also received the order to advance on the 18th to Kuttlau. Only the corps' heavy baggage remained at Grüneberg' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 22).

claims.value: Side A: Marshal Davout's letter of 4 November reports that his officer wrote from Beuthen that all Silesia was without Prussian troops except the fortresses and that the garrison of Glogau amounted to 3,500 men, of whom 1,000 cavalry, under Major General Margitz, who was said to be very uneasy and mediocre. The major general's letter of 5 November had Deroy send cavalry parties toward Breslau to intercept the couriers and learn the situation of that place, and the Emperor wrote on 10 November that Lefebvre ought to have sent Jérôme more information on what had happened in the country. Höpfner: on 8 November the engineer officer with Lefebvre reconnoitred the place and found it in a state that permitted a forcible attack, but the corps' troops were too little known for it; deserters brought side A the most exact news of the state of the works, which led to the plan of a coup de main; and the rumour of the approach of a Russian corps 10,000 men strong gave occasion to a concentration of the corps. The 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November, counted one regiment of the King of Prussia in Gross-Glogau.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and Bulletin, read from the page images, with Höpfner. The passages read do not show what side A knew of the garrison's true strength or of its unreliability before the deserters came, or what Lefebvre reported; Davout's figures are also in claim side-b-strength-other. The engineer officer's judgement and the deserters' news are Höpfner's account, without a cited report. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor. Francfort, 4 November 1806'; 'I received this morning a report from one of my officers whom I sent toward Breslau with 80 horse to stop the couriers and get news; he writes to me from Beuthen on the Oder, a few leagues from Glogau, that all Silesia is without Prussian' (the word continues on p. 42; the note mark refers to Foucart's footnote, not transcribed); 'troops, except the fortresses; that the garrison of Glogau amounts to 3,500 men, of whom 1,000 cavalry. It is composed, like that of Küstrin, of 3rd battalions. Major General Margitz commands the place. He is said to be very uneasy and mediocre' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 41); 'the Major General to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 5 November 1806'; 'the Emperor orders that Your Highness send' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'General Deroy to invest the place of Glogau with 6,000 men... Your Highness will prescribe to General Deroy to have himself scouted for and to send cavalry parties toward Breslau to intercept the couriers and learn thereby the situation of that place..... General Deroy will be before Glogau on the 7th or 8th at the latest; you on the 6th in the evening at Grüneberg; the Württembergers on the 7th at Zullichau in position' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 56; the points are the print's); 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: since 30 October Glogau had been prepared for Bavarian troops being destined for Silesia; on 7 November at 2 in the afternoon mounted messengers from the neighbouring villages reported the enemy's approach, and the reconnaissance toward Herrendorf met numerous troops of enemy cavalry. At the parley of 8 November side A communicated that Stettin and Küstrin had fallen and the Prussian army was shattered; a later summons communicated army orders announcing the surrender of Küstrin and Magdeburg. After the bombardment of 1 December Vandamme assured the governor that no relief could be hoped for, since neither a Prussian nor a Russian army stood on this side of the Vistula and the King of Prussia was already in Russia, and, as the governor would not believe it, gave his word of honour in writing. Höpfner says the government knew the investing troops were comparatively very weak, and that the royal order of 2 November, demanding a defence to the last man, had been communicated to it.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. The passages read do not show whether the governor knew of the suspension of arms of 16 November, whose article 2 named Glogau (claim side-a-objectives), or what he knew of side A's strength beyond Höpfner's statement; the royal order of 2 November was not seen. Vandamme's assurance and the army orders are side A's communications, kept as Höpfner gives them. English renderings (ours): 'since 30 October Glogau had been prepared for Bavarian troops being destined for Silesia'; 'on 7 November at 2 in the afternoon mounted messengers from the neighbouring villages brought the report that the enemy was approaching, and at 3½ the foot and mounted Jäger and the cavalry moved out in the direction of Herrendorf to reconnoitre'; 'this detachment was a few thousand paces from the works when it already came upon numerous troops of enemy cavalry, and had to fall back on the fortress after the loss of 4 prisoners'; 'on the morning of 8 November at 6 o'clock the cannonade against the fortress was continued, during which the' (the sentence continues on p. 20); 'engineer officer attached to the detachment reconnoitred the place and found it in a state that well permitted a forcible attack. Since, however, the troops of the corps were too little known as to their competence to entrust them with an undertaking still so hazardous, he asked only for the building of 5-6 batteries of 8-10 guns, above all high-angle pieces, to bombard works and town' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 19); 'at 11 o'clock, after the cannonade, there was a parley anew, with the communication that Stettin and Küstrin had fallen and the Prussian army was shattered'; 'a further summons, in which Jerome declared that he would lay waste the town in the most terrible manner if the capitulation were not accepted, and at the same time communicated army orders announcing the surrender of Küstrin and Magdeburg, was again rejected'; 'on 1 December at 6¼ in the morning the bombardment began and lasted until after 9 o'clock. The garrison's artillery had indeed answered with vigour, but the enemy had achieved his purpose. The certainty that siege guns had arrived, that the enemy had it in his power to burn the town to ashes, had completely changed the government's mind'; 'immediately after the end of the fire General Vandamme sent a parlementaire anew and summoned the fortress with the assurance that no relief was to be hoped for, since neither a Prussian nor a Russian army stood on this side of the Vistula and the King of Prussia was already in Russia. Since the governor would not believe these statements, the French general gave his word of honour in writing for further confirmation'; 'even if these reasons must in themselves be recognised as correct, they have not the slightest force to justify a capitulation, since the government knew that the investing troops were comparatively very weak, and the royal order of 2 November communicated to it expressly demanded a defence to the last man'.
