claims.value: Side A: Höpfner says Napoleon wished early on to take Glogau quickly, because with Stettin and Küstrin it completed the basing on the Oder for the advance over the Vistula and its possession opened a direct connection from southern Germany by way of Dresden to South Prussia, and that Lefebvre was sent on 6 November to move the commandant to surrender by the surprising appearance of his cavalry, as at Erfurt and Stettin. The major general's letter of 5 November sent Deroy to invest Glogau with 6,000 men and to be before it on the 7th or 8th at the latest. The Emperor wrote on 10 November that he greatly wished to be master of Glogau and was sending mortars and howitzers to bombard the town, and that once Glogau was invested Jérôme should send cavalry toward Breslau. The major general wrote on 16 November that the Württembergers were to blockade the town on the right bank, with 2,000 Württemberg infantry, all their cavalry and 4 guns sent to Lissa to put themselves in correspondence with Marshal Davout's troops at Posen, and all the Bavarians to unite on the left: the Emperor must have Glogau, whatever it cost, so the place was to be strictly blockaded, and a bridge was to be thrown over the Oder near Glogau to favour the blockade; one Bavarian division was to advance toward Breslau to Parchwitz or Lüben. Berthier answered Jérôme's report on the abandoned storm that Deroy's observations were very just, that a town could not be taken by assault without a breach where there was an escarp and a good counterscarp, and that those who favoured such an attack were very wrong. Höpfner: the infantry's approach from the 19th was ordered by Napoleon to unsettle the garrison and make it inclined to surrender, and Napoleon continually pressed Jérôme to hasten the capture. The suspension of arms signed at Charlottenburg on 16 November, printed with the 33rd Bulletin of 17 November, provided in article 2 that the French troops would occupy in Silesia the places of Glogau and Breslau, and in article 4 that the places named in article 2 would be handed over within the eight days following the exchange of ratifications, their garrisons not to be prisoners of war but directed on Kœnigsberg; ratifications were to be exchanged at Graudenz at the latest on the 21st, and by Foucart's note hostilities were to cease only then; the 35th Bulletin, of 28 November, says the King of Prussia told Duroc that he could not ratify it. The major general's letter of 22 November sent Deroy's and Wrede's divisions to Kalisch from the 24th and entrusted the blockade of Glogau to Vandamme and the Württembergers; Foucart cites an order of 27 November to Vandamme to go before Glogau.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, the French letters and the Bulletins, read from the page images. The aims moved from a surprise by cavalry (6-7 November) through investment and bombardment to a strict blockade at any cost (16 November), with the unratified suspension of arms of 16 November offering Glogau by treaty, and then to a blockade by one division under Vandamme (22 November); they came from the Emperor and from the commanders, so the phase is left unresolved. Berthier's answer on the storm is quoted only in Höpfner's footnote, in French; the letter was not seen in Foucart. The passages read do not show whether Jérôme or the garrison knew of the suspension. The sentence on hostilities is Foucart's note, not the suspension's text. English renderings (ours): 'Napoleon had wished early on to make himself master of the fortress of Glogau quickly, because, with Stettin and Küstrin, it completed the basing on the Oder for the further advance over the Vistula, and the possession of Glogau opened a direct connection from southern Germany by way of Dresden to South Prussia'; 'as early as 6 November General Lefebvre had been set in march to that end with his brigade and a light battery on the left bank of the Oder against Glogau, to move the commandant to surrender by the surprising appearance of this cavalry, as had succeeded so splendidly at Erfurt and Stettin'; 'the Major General to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 5 November 1806'; 'the Emperor orders that Your Highness send' (the sentence continues on p. 57); 'General Deroy to invest the place of Glogau with 6,000 men... Your Highness will prescribe to General Deroy to have himself scouted for and to send cavalry parties toward Breslau to intercept the couriers and learn thereby the situation of that place..... General Deroy will be before Glogau on the 7th or 8th at the latest; you on the 6th in the evening at Grüneberg; the Württembergers on the 7th at Zullichau in position' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 56; the points are the print's); 'the Emperor to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 10 November 1806'; 'I greatly wish to be master of Glogau. I have given orders to the general commanding at Küstrin to embark 6 mortars and 4 siege howitzers and to send them to you to bombard the town. If Glogau surrenders, send an officer to inform Küstrin of it, so that this movement is not made'; 'from the moment that Glogau is invested by General Deroy, send cavalry parties toward Breslau, and, as it is possible that the enemy has men there, send a considerable force on both banks. You may continue to charge your two French brigade generals, with their corps, with this mission'; 'the Major General to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'the Emperor charges me to inform Your Imperial Highness that you are to keep the Württemberg troops on the right bank of the Oder and the Bavarian troops on the left bank. Order the Württemberg troops to move before Glogau and blockade that town on the right bank; send 2,000 men of Württemberg infantry, all the cavalry of that nation and 4 pieces of artillery to Lissa, from where it will put itself in correspondence at once with the troops of Marshal Davout who are at Posen;'; 'as I told you, unite all the Bavarians on the left bank: the Emperor must have Glogau, whatever it costs; so have that place strictly blockaded'; 'the Emperor wishes you to have a bridge thrown over the Oder near Glogau; this bridge will have the double advantage of favouring your blockade and giving you the means of moving rapidly from one bank to the other'; 'have one of the Bavarian divisions advance from Glogau toward Breslau, which can keep itself at Parchwitz or at Lüben; from there it will make it easier for you to get subsistence and will be able to support the cavalry that will be before Breslau'; '1) on Jerome's report of the abandonment of the storm Napoleon had Marshal Berthier answer: "I have put your letter before the Emperor, Monseigneur; His Majesty finds that the observations General Deroy made to you are very just; one cannot take a town by assault when one has not made the breach and when there is an escarp and a good counterscarp; His Majesty thinks that those who could be of the opinion of such an attack were very greatly wrong; for one would lose many men uselessly there."'; 'the enemy gradually approached the works with his infantry in small pits and opened his musket fire on the 19th, so that the bullets flew into the town'; 'these arrangements on the enemy's side had been made on Napoleon's order, to unsettle the garrison day and night thereby and make it worn down and inclined to surrender'; 'continually pressed by Napoleon to hasten the capture of Glogau, Jerome was about to attempt an attack on the bridgehead on the right bank of the Oder; but circumstances arose that prevented the execution. Jerome received, that is, the order to leave only one division before Glogau and to set out with the rest of the corps with all speed against Kalisch'; '1. 33rd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 17 November 1806' (the '1.' is the footnote's mark); 'the attached suspension of arms was signed yesterday at Charlottenburg'; 'Art. 2. — The troops of His Majesty the Emperor of the French, King of Italy, shall occupy the part of southern Prussia lying on the right bank of the Vistula as far as the mouth of the Bug, Thorn, the fortress and town of Graudenz, the town and citadel of Danzig, the places of Colberg and Lenczyc, which shall be handed over to them for security; and in Silesia, the places of Glogau and Breslau, with the portion of that province lying on the right bank of the Oder, and the part of it lying on the left bank of the same river which shall have as its limit a line resting on that river 5 leagues above Breslau, passing by Ohlau and Zobten, 3 leagues behind Schweidnitz and without including it, and from there to Freyburg and Landshut, and joining Bohemia at Liebau'; 'Art. 4. — The places of Hameln and Nienburg, as well as those designated in article 2, shall be handed over to the French troops with their armament and munitions, of which an inventory shall be drawn up, within the eight days following the exchange of the ratifications of the present suspension of arms. The garrisons of these places shall not be prisoners of war; they shall be directed on Kœnigsberg, and they shall be given every facility necessary for this'; 'Art. 6. — The present suspension of arms shall be ratified by the two high contracting powers, and the exchange of ratifications shall take place at Graudenz at the latest on the 21st of the present month'; 'done at Charlottenburg, 16 November 1806'; 'hostilities were to cease only at the moment of the exchange of ratifications'; '35th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Posen, 28 November 1806'; 'the marshal of the palace, Duroc, went as far as Osterode, where he saw the King of Prussia, who declared to him that part of his states was occupied by the Russians and that he was entirely in their dependence; that consequently he could not ratify the suspension of arms that his plenipotentiaries had concluded, because he could not carry out its stipulations'; 'the Major General to Prince Jérôme. Berlin, 22 November 1806, one o'clock in the afternoon'; 'the Emperor orders you to have General Deroy's Bavarian division leave, on the 24th, the position it occupies before Glogau to go to Kalisch, where His Majesty's intention is that it arrive on the 27th or 28th'; 'you will likewise have the 2nd Bavarian division, called General de Wrède's, leave Parchwitz on the same day, the 24th, to be likewise at Kalisch on the 27th or 28th at the latest'; 'His Majesty orders that the blockade of Glogau be entrusted to General Vandamme and to the Württemberg troops under his orders'; '1. order to General Vandamme to go before Glogau (Major General, Meseritz, 27 November 1806, 5 in the morning)' (Foucart's footnote).

claims.value: Side B (Prussian): the governor's answer that Puttlitz carried on 14 November, as Höpfner prints it in French, said that he was not permitted to make use of the prince's goodwill before fulfilling his duties to the King his master, and that when he should see the impossibility of defending the fortress any longer he hoped for an equitable and honourable capitulation. Höpfner: the royal order of 2 November, communicated to the government, expressly demanded a defence to the last man. After the bombardment of 1 December the governor, who had shortly before declared that he would let himself be buried under the ruins of the town, proposed a capitulation with free withdrawal, which Vandamme rejected; the government's reasons for surrender were the insufficiency of the garrison for the works, the unreliability of the battalions made up of Poles, the arrival of the siege guns and the impossibility of relief.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. The aims moved from defence, under the royal order, to capitulation on the best terms obtainable; they came from the King's order and from the governor and government, so the phase is left unresolved. Höpfner's report, from French statements, that the governor recognised on the 13th the impossibility of defending himself (claim side-b-command) stands beside the letter he prints, which promises a capitulation only when that impossibility is seen (our comparison). The royal order of 2 November was not seen. English renderings (ours): 'the brave Major Puttlitz, commander of the 3rd musketeer battalion of vac. Grevenitz, who had spoken out most decidedly against the capitulation, was charged at 2 in the afternoon of the 14th with carrying the refusal to the enemy'; '1) the answer ran: "Monseigneur! General Lefebvre, whom Your Imperial Highness sent into the place, has made me the proposal with which you charged him. I am deeply touched by the sentiments of benevolence and goodness that Your Imperial Highness has been pleased to show both for the garrison and for the inhabitants of the town, but I am not permitted to make use of them before having fulfilled the duties I owe the King my master. I am convinced that His Majesty the Emperor as well as Your Imperial Highness know how to esteem him who, even in misfortune, fulfils his duties." "When I should see the impossibility of defending any longer the fortress entrusted to me, I hope that Your Imperial Highness will be pleased still to grant me an equitable and honourable capitulation."'; 'even if these reasons must in themselves be recognised as correct, they have not the slightest force to justify a capitulation, since the government knew that the investing troops were comparatively very weak, and the royal order of 2 November communicated to it expressly demanded a defence to the last man'; 'on 1 December at 6¼ in the morning the bombardment began and lasted until after 9 o'clock. The garrison's artillery had indeed answered with vigour, but the enemy had achieved his purpose. The certainty that siege guns had arrived, that the enemy had it in his power to burn the town to ashes, had completely changed the government's mind'; 'although the governor had shortly before fallen out with Major Puttlitz over entering into a capitulation and on that occasion had declared that he would let himself be buried under the ruins of the town, he now nevertheless proposed to the enemy a capitulation with free withdrawal. General Vandamme rejected this proposal, and the governor promised to make other proposals the next day'; 'the reasons that moved the government to surrender were the following: 1) the insufficiency of the garrison for the defence of the works that necessarily had to be held; 2) the unreliability of the 3rd battalions of Tschepe and Zastrow, made up of Poles, whose commanders had themselves declared that they could no longer rely on their men; 3) the arrival of the enemy's siege guns, by which the complete ruin of the town would have been unavoidable, and 4) the impossibility of a relief'.

claims.value: Side A attacked: Bodart has the Bavarians and French force the garrison to surrender after a 15-day blockade. Höpfner: Lefebvre's cavalry and light battery came before the fortress on 7 November and enclosed it on both banks; Deroy's division enclosed it on the 10th; side A bombarded the town on the 13th, 15th and 16th of November and on 1 December, summoned the fortress repeatedly, approached the works with infantry in small pits from the 19th, gave up a planned storm, and received the capitulation on 2 December and the formal handover on the 3rd. Side B stopped all sorties that could give occasion for desertion, but on 18 November a detachment raided the Grundmühle, and on 22 November troops went into the nearest outworks to take the enemy's pits in flank and rear.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A invested, bombarded and summoned the fortress, and side B, apart from a raid and a move into the outworks, defended it until it capitulated. The phase is left unresolved: the investment followed the Emperor's and Jérôme's orders, while the summonses, the bombardments and the terms were the commanders' own (claims side-a-command, side-a-objectives). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'two squadrons of Chevauxlegers crossed to the right bank of the Oder at Neusalz, so as to be able to invest the fortress on both banks on 7 November'; 'the canister fire from the works drove the Bavarian cavalry back toward Prostau, and they contented themselves with enclosing the fortress on both banks and summoning it by two parlementaires. The governor rejected the proposals'; 'as soon as Jerome had received General Lefebvre's report, he made all arrangements to enter Silesia now. The division Deroy had to advance from Krossen to Glogau on 9 November, so as to enclose the place on the 10th with the brigade Raglowich on the left bank and with the brigade Siebein on the right bank'; 'on the 13th at 4 in the morning the enemy opened his fire on both banks, although the darkness allowed aiming only at the fire of the fortress batteries, which answered with liveliness. The town burned in thirteen different places, but everywhere the fires were soon put out'; 'on the 15th the fire of the blockading troops began anew at 4½ in the morning and lasted until 9 o'clock. In the town two houses burned down'; 'on 16 November at 4½ in the morning the enemy's fire began anew on both banks of the Oder. The town burned in perhaps 30 places, but through the exemplary conduct of the burghers, supported by some men detailed for it, the fire was this time too put out everywhere'; 'on 1 December at 6¼ in the morning the bombardment began and lasted until after 9 o'clock. The garrison's artillery had indeed answered with vigour, but the enemy had achieved his purpose. The certainty that siege guns had arrived, that the enemy had it in his power to burn the town to ashes, had completely changed the government's mind'; 'the enemy gradually approached the works with his infantry in small pits and opened his musket fire on the 19th, so that the bullets flew into the town'; 'fascines, ladders etc., everything lay ready, when at the moment of execution General Deroy declared that he did not believe he could count on his troops for so doubtful an undertaking, since they, not used to such hazardous attacks, might easily lack the boldness and energy that alone make success certain. The storm had to be given up and the siege guns awaited'; 'on 2 December the government now had new points of capitulation drafted, without calling the prescribed formal council of war, and when at noon the copies were not yet ready, an officer was sent to General Vandamme to apologise for this delay. The officer sent returned with General Vandamme's general staff officer and proposals of capitulation that agreed in essentials with those of the government. Agreement was therefore now reached very soon, and that same evening the Breslau and Oder gates were occupied by the Württembergers'; 'on 3 December the fortress was formally handed over. The troops marched out and laid down on the glacis their muskets, which had mostly been broken beforehand. The invalids were released, the remaining men transported as prisoners of war'; 'on the garrison's side all works, sorties etc. that could give occasion for desertion were stopped, since the losses by desertion would very soon have weakened the garrison to the utmost'; 'on 18 November the fortress artillery tried to set on fire the water mill lying nearest the Sternschanze, the so-called Grundmühle, which gave shelter to a Bavarian post, but did not achieve its aim'; 'under the lead of the place's engineer officer a detachment of 1 officer, 40 men of the 3rd battalion von Grevenitz and some artillerymen with pitch wreaths went forward to the mill, quickly occupied the exit of the buildings, took prisoner after slight resistance the enemy post, surprised, of 1 officer and 23 men of the 4th Line Regiment, set the buildings on fire and returned to the fortress. The miller, however, managed to save the mill'; 'at last on 22 November, when the enemy had approached with his pits especially along the avenue of Rauschwitz, Lieutenant Sommerfeld was sent forward with the detachment of the regiment Zenge into the nearest outworks, and on the proposal of the place's engineer a 12-pounder was brought into the counterguard of the Prussian ravelin, so as to take the' (the sentence continues on p. 27); 'advanced enemy in flank and rear. To the same end the garrison's Jäger went into the outworks to the right of the ravelin toward the Oder. The enemy infantry fire was markedly quenched by this and in the following days kept up only moderately' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 26).

claims.value: Side B held a permanent fortress on both banks of the Oder. Höpfner: the palisading could not be completed and only the weakest places were secured, work going on during the investment; the mass of the outworks was given up and the defence restricted to the main wall, since the garrison seemed too weak and unreliable and the guns too few, and the outworks were so low that they had little defensibility and, being impossible to palisade, would only have favoured desertion; the garrison held the main wall on the left bank, the Dom-Retranchement on the right bank and the Sternschanze, with patrols in the abandoned outworks; on 22 November troops went back into the nearest outworks and a 12-pounder into the counterguard of the Prussian ravelin. At the fall the walls had suffered nothing. Side A: Lefebvre used the night after his arrival to have two earthworks raised to cover his guns, later called batteries No. 4 and 5; on 11 November the Bavarians worked on the left bank at cover for six batteries, built more solidly after the refusal and repaired under the fortress's fire; in the night to the 18th they worked at trenches of about 100 paces to the right and left of the batteries, to hold 200 infantry each to cover the artillery; from the 19th the infantry approached in small pits. Höpfner nevertheless says that Glogau fell without side A having opened any siege works.
claims.rationale: Coded both_fortified: side B defended permanent works, and side A placed its guns behind earthworks and held trenches and pits under the fortress's fire. The fortress is permanent (inherited); side A's works were made for the blockade on its commanders' dispositions (commander-created); one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. A coding that counted only the defended fortress would give B_fortified. Höpfner's statement that side A opened no siege works is kept beside his account of its trenches and pits; we read it as meaning no formal siege approaches against the works (our reading). Höpfner's Plan Nr. XVII was not inspected. English renderings (ours): 'the palisading could not be completed despite all activity; it had only been possible to secure the weakest places, but work went on with effort even during the investment'; 'the mass of the outworks had been given up and the defence restricted rather to the main wall, since the garrison seemed too weak and too unreliable and the number of guns too small, and at the same time the outworks were so low that they had little defensibility and, being impossible to palisade, would only have favoured desertion'; 'the most reliable battalion of the garrison, the battalion von Grevenitz, occupied the weakest places of the main wall on the left bank of the Oder, the less reliable battalion von Tschepe the rest of it, and the worst battalion, von Zastrow, the Dom-Retranchement [the cathedral entrenchment] on the right bank of the Oder; a detachment of the best invalids held the Sternschanze [star fort] at the fortress's upper junction with the Oder, the rest of the invalids occupied the gorge' (the sentence continues on p. 19); 'of this work; the cavalry and the Jäger were used to patrol the abandoned outworks. The burghers did duty in the town' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 18); 'at last on 22 November, when the enemy had approached with his pits especially along the avenue of Rauschwitz, Lieutenant Sommerfeld was sent forward with the detachment of the regiment Zenge into the nearest outworks, and on the proposal of the place's engineer a 12-pounder was brought into the counterguard of the Prussian ravelin, so as to take the' (the sentence continues on p. 27); 'advanced enemy in flank and rear. To the same end the garrison's Jäger went into the outworks to the right of the ravelin toward the Oder. The enemy infantry fire was markedly quenched by this and in the following days kept up only moderately' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 26); 'so fell Glogau, without the enemy having opened any siege works or dared a storm. The walls had suffered nothing at all; the damage to the burghers' houses was comparatively slight; the fortress artillery was in completely good condition, despite the place's artillery officer having stated the contrary;' (the sentence continues on p. 30); 'General Lefebvre soon recognised that he would achieve nothing with the cavalry alone, and reported at once to headquarters on the result of his mission, but used the night to have two earthworks raised by country people brought together, to cover the guns he had brought with him'; '1) later called batteries No. 4 and 5'; 'on 11 November the Bavarians worked on the left bank at cover for six batteries, and on the evening of the 12th the artillery of the division Wrede also arrived from Grüneberg before Glogau. At midnight the guns were brought into these earthworks, each of them, with the exception of battery No. 5, armed with 4 cannon and 2 howitzers; the said' (the sentence continues on p. 21); 'the gun cover was built more solidly, and since the fortress's 6-pounders did no damage but did betray the weakness of the blockading troops' artillery, it was decided to restrict themselves more to the use of the howitzers and 12-pounders and to arm the batteries accordingly, so that batteries No. 2, 3 and 4 were each equipped with two 12-pounders and 2 howitzers, battery No. 1 with two 12-pounders, and only battery No. 5 with two 6-pounders and 1 howitzer, while battery No. 6 was given up entirely'; 'the fortress answered more lively than on the 13th and did the cover considerable damage, so that here and there the guns had to be withdrawn onto the open field and the cover' (the sentence continues on p. 24); 'repaired, while the fortress harassed the workers with its fire' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 23); 'in the night to the 18th the blockading troops worked on the left bank of the Oder at trenches about 100 paces long, to the right and left of the several batteries, so as to place in them 200 men of infantry each to cover the artillery,' (the sentence continues on p. 26); 'and everything was prepared for setting up the mortars and heavy howitzers expected from Küstrin, which had been embarked on the 14th but were held up by the water level of the Oder' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 25); 'the enemy gradually approached the works with his infantry in small pits and opened his musket fire on the 19th, so that the bullets flew into the town'.

open_questions: Deferred: Höpfner's Plan Nr. XVII of Glogau, not inspected; the part of Höpfner's chapter 15 before p. 15, on the first measures for the defence of Silesia, not read beyond its heading and first page in the OCR; the continuation of the major general's letter of 22 November on Foucart, Campagne de Pologne, t. I, p. 146, which concerns the Württemberg cavalry left toward Breslau and Jérôme's move to Kalisch, kept for the Breslau entry; the capitulation's text, the royal order of 2 November, Berthier's letter on the abandoned storm (seen only in Höpfner's footnote), and Jérôme's and Lefebvre's reports, not found in the pages read; and the contemporary account of the siege of Breslau in the Lower Silesian Digital Library, kept for the Breslau entry. No figure seen only in the OCR is restated.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength and composition at the capitulation. Höpfner's Württemberg division of about 8000 men, from which the major general's letter of 16 November ordered 2,000 infantry, all the cavalry and 4 guns to Lissa, and Montbrun's cavalry at Polkwitz are the only figures for the force under Vandamme, and Bodart's 8,000 Bavarians and 1,000 French match no body of troops before Glogau in the passages read. A return of the Württemberg division or Vandamme's report on the capitulation could close it.

Disputes kept as separate claims or within them: the garrison (3228 men and 124 guns, Höpfner; 3,200 men and 124 guns, Bodart; 3,500 including 1,000 cavalry, Davout's officer; one regiment, the 32nd Bulletin); side A at the capitulation (9,000, of them 1,000 French, under Deroy, Bodart; Deroy's division gone on the 25th and the Württembergers under Vandamme taking the capitulation, Höpfner and the order of 22 November); the first force before Glogau (Lefebvre's brigade and a light battery, Höpfner; 3 cavalry regiments and 6 pieces, Foucart's narrative; 2,000 horse, the 30th Bulletin); Deroy's investment (the 10th, Höpfner; the 9th, the 30th Bulletin); the first bombardment (on the 8th by 10 howitzers, the 30th Bulletin; a cannonade on the 7th and 8th and the first fire from six batteries on the 13th, Höpfner); the siege guns (6 mortars and 4 howitzers ordered, the Emperor; 6 small and 4 heavy mortars and 4 heavy howitzers, Höpfner); the governor's answer of the 13th and 14th (that he recognised the impossibility of defence, by French statements, Höpfner's text; a refusal, the letter in his footnote); the siege works (none opened, Höpfner's verdict; batteries, trenches and pits, his narrative); the day of the capitulation (2 December, Bodart; agreed on the 2nd and handed over on the 3rd, Höpfner); and the prisoners (the garrison captive with the officers on parole, Bodart; the invalids released and the rest prisoners, Höpfner).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked; his 124 guns agree with Höpfner's, his 3,200 men are not Höpfner's 3228 rounded up, and his 1,000 French match no troop body in the passages read); Foucart, Campagne de Prusse, t. II, and Campagne de Pologne, t. I, one family (the same author's editions of the French side's documents, from the page images: Davout's letter of 4 November, the major general's letters to Jérôme of 5, 16 and 22 November, the Emperor's to Jérôme of 10 November and to the Grand Duke of Berg of 3 December, the 30th, 32nd, 33rd and 35th Bulletins, the suspension of arms of 16 November printed with the 33rd, and Foucart's narrative on p. 68); Höpfner, Bd. 4 (the Prussian side's history, the same work and family as his first and second volumes; he cites no document for the garrison's strength, the councils or the capitulation's terms, marks the governor's answer of the 13th as given by French statements, and prints the governor's letter and Berthier's answer in French). Völderndorff's Bavarian history, the account of side A's Bavarian divisions (fourth book, pp. 56-66; pp. 59-60, 63 not read), was read on the page images and not used: the brief allows two families besides Bodart, and the group's two campaign families were kept.
